title: The Stoic Letters, 16th November
summary: Set Your Own Clock: The case against the 5 a.m. alarm
body_markdown:
Dear Stoics,


Have you ever closed an app feeling worse than when you opened it? Someone fit and glowing has just shown you their morning: up at 4, head to the gym or out for a run, chug a glass of something green, swallow a row of supplements, then take an everything shower, plus twenty more steps you lost count of. And the clock still hasn’t reached 8 a.m. Meanwhile, you are on your second snooze, wondering what is wrong with you. We’re here to remind you that nothing is wrong with you.


Let’s begin with something that should be common knowledge by now: social media is a highlight reel, edited, well lit and sponsored by brands. But there is an even better reason to let those videos go: rising before dawn is only one way to live well, and for many of us


[it isn’t the best one](https://www.rnz.co.nz/life/wellbeing/the-5am-myth-waking-early-won-t-make-you-more-successful)


. Each of us has an inner clock that was set long before we started wishing for the perfect morning routine. Whether you come alive at sunrise or late in the evening is


[written partly into your DNA](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6200828/)


. The clock changes with age, too. Teenagers need to sleep in, while most of us start our days earlier as the years pass.


The part the influencers don’t tell you about is that larks don’t sleep better than owls. The only difference is that they go to sleep and wake up earlier. For many of us, later is actually the healthier choice. A night owl’s body reaches its best hours in the evening, when the mind is clearest and the muscles are strongest. This is around the time early risers are already winding down.


[Owls are every bit as sharp](https://www.psypost.org/night-owls-show-higher-cognitive-performance-in-new-sleep-study/)


as early birds, and on tests of memory and reasoning they often come out a little ahead. Drag that same owl out of bed at 5 a.m. and they will think through fog and be in a bad mood all day. There’s absolutely no reason for them to adopt a routine built for someone else’s body and mind.


Now it’s time to go back to basics. What you really need is


**enough sleep**


(which for most adults means seven to nine hours, although a lucky few are built to feel great on six) and


**the kind of sleep that leaves you rested**


, because the feeling of rest shapes our happiness and health more than any number on a tracker. Then there is a


**steady rhythm**


, with bedtime and wake-up time roughly the same from day to day. And lastly,


**the familiar routine**


: a nourishing breakfast, a lighter dinner, little or no alcohol, some sunlight and movement during your day.


You only need to discover what is missing from your routine and how to adjust it to your work, family and anything else that matters to you. Maybe your best ideas just arrive at 9 p.m., which is completely fine. When do you feel most awake? When does your body ask for rest? Could you live like this for years? Follow the answers and find your own comfortable rhythm, even when it looks nothing like anyone else’s. You know yourself best.


Someone wise once said that you have to love yourself first to be able to love others. Perhaps it starts with letting yourself wake up the way you were built to. Be gentle and kind to yourself this week.


Yours truly,


The Stoic App Team


#### If a man does not keep pace with his companions, perhaps it is because he hears a different drummer. Let him step to the music which he hears, however measured or far away.


*Henry David Thoreau, “Walden”*


We are quick to list our flaws and slow to name what we do well. This week, we’ll practise the kind of pride that needs no audience, and take time to celebrate our strengths, achievements and the things we worked hard for.


What is something you’re proud of that very few people know about? When did you last feel genuinely proud of yourself? What would you love to be complimented on more often?


[Open Stoic](https://www.newsletter.getstoic.com/p/getstoic.com/explore/weekly-themes)


and give yourself the credit you deserve.
